## Introduction

Less than 100 miles from the Mid-Atlantic coast, the ocean floor descends dramatically through a range of massive canyons down to the abyss of the deep sea. Deep in these canyons hide extraordinary undersea worlds just beginning to be explored.

Residents of Norfolk, VA, Baltimore, MD, and the New York City area’s Hudson River Valley may be surprised to learn that not far from their shores exist underwater communities that not only share the names of the places they live, but are just as bustling and diverse. Hundreds to thousands of meters below the surface of the ocean, the dark and icy-cold waters of deep-sea canyons are indeed not the habitat most would associate with diverse underwater ecosystems. However, submarine canyons, like those found in the Mid-Atlantic, can contain some of the most productive deep-sea habitats, hosting remarkably high biological abundance and diversity.

Powered by [Esri]

Mid-Atlantic Canyons

This story map explores three of the largest deep-sea canyons that incise (cut into) the Mid-Atlantic continental shelf and slope, including information about their topography and the diversity of marine life that call them home.

Before we explore these truly grand canyons individually, let’s take a brief moment to learn a little more about deep-sea canyons and coral ecosystems and how they are being studied.

## Deep-Sea Topography

Deep below the surface of the ocean, there are mountains and canyons much larger than those on land, and, just as mountains and canyons on land can affect air flow and influence weather patterns, their submarine counterparts can affect the ocean’s circulation. The immense walls of deep-sea canyons act like massive funnels. Ocean currents accelerate as they are channeled through the relatively narrow canyons and the food supplies they carry, such as plankton and other organic particles, are concentrated.

![Image 3](blob:https://gaia.vcu.edu/10f088b0-7db5-4875-b4a1-54f7684c3e38)

Manuscript painting of Heezen-Tharp World ocean floor mapby Berann.

In addition to transporting the essential nutrients forming the base of the food chain in the canyons, these strong currents create a unique and rugged environment, continually scouring the craggy walls clean of sediment. The availability of hard surfaces (rocks and compacted muds) which they require in order to anchor themselves, along with an abundant supply of food, make submarine canyons an ideal habitat for deep-sea corals.

Along with plentiful food supplies, topography and depth drive diversity and abundance in deep-sea canyons. Canyons that cut deeply into the edge of the continental shelf are referred to as “incised.” Ocean currents that have accelerated from flowing through incised canyons transport more suspended organic materials than in their non-incised counterparts. This greater supply of organic materials allows incised canyons to host greater productivity and support more abundant and diverse deep-sea coral ecosystems.

While corals do occur often at shallower depths, and can even be found over a mile deep, the greatest diversity and abundance of deep-sea corals thrive from 300 to 800 meters below the surface.

## Deep Sea Exploration

![Image 4]

Scientists identifying targets for a remotely operated vehicle dive. (Image courtesy of Deepwater Canyons - Pathways to the Abyss)

![Image 5]

Crew members hoisting the ROV Jason II into the water to explore Norfolk Canyon. (Image courtesy of Deepwater Canyons - Pathways to the Abyss)

According to the [Mid-Atlantic Regional Council on the Ocean], submarine canyons are the next great American frontier, possessing untapped potential for exploration and research. By studying these canyons, scientists are beginning to increase our understanding of the role they play in ocean ecosystems, the benefits they provide to human populations, and how the sensitive habitats within the canyons may be impacted by human activities.

Over the last decade, scientists from federal agencies, academic institutions, and nonprofits have journeyed to the continental shelf and slope aboard specialized research vessels to explore the deep. Earlier missions focused on creating new detailed three-dimensional maps of the sea floor and canyon walls using multibeam sonars. These maps allowed later missions to pilot remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) with cameras and other equipment through the canyons to study the unique habitats and fascinating marine life that make their home in these dark and cold oases of the deep.

![Image 6]

The control room of the NOAA ship Okeanos Explorer, shown in the large image below. (NOAA)

![Image 7]

NOAA Okeanos Explorer Research Vessel. (NOAA)

Let's now travel to the first canyon on our journey to learn more about the amazing diversity of life these explorations have uncovered.

## Norfolk Canyon

We start our journey about 70 miles east of Virginia’s Atlantic coast, where a sharp gouge in the edge of the continental shelf marks the head of the southernmost of the region’s large canyons. How large? Norfolk Canyon stretches over 35 miles and its steep, craggy walls descend over a mile to some 6,000 feet -- the same as the deepest part of the Grand Canyon!

Better Known Canyons

There are several possibilities explaining the formation of what is now Norfolk Canyon. Geologists believe it was either carved by turbidity flows, ancient rivers, or possibly was eroded by waves as sea levels rose after the last ice age.

![Image 8]

Basket stars rest on a pink bubblegum coral in Norfolk Canyon. The white coral on the right is _Lophelia pertusa_, newly discovered in the Mid-Atlantic. (Image courtesy of Deepwater Canyons - Pathways to the Abyss)

![Image 9]

A black coral growing on a vertical wall at about 1200 meter depth in Norfolk Canyon, and the deep-water catshark _Apristurus manis_. (Image courtesy of Deepwater Canyons - Pathways to the Abyss)

Although only a small portion of Norfolk canyon has been explored, more than a half-dozen cold-water coral species have been observed so far, including dominant tree coral, _Paragorgia arborea_. Norfolk Canyon is also home to the stony (reef-building) coral _Lophelia pertusa_, that had not been observed anywhere in the Mid-Atlantic until [recent explorations of these canyons]. These corals, accompanied by various species of anemones and sponges, provide critical habitat for all kinds of sea creatures, including over 120 species of fishes identified in Norfolk Canyon.

![Image 10]

A small cluster of _Lophelia pertusa_ coral growing on a vertical rock wall in Norfolk Canyon. (Image courtesy of Deepwater Canyons - Pathways to the Abyss)

At the base of Norfolk Canyon, almost a mile deep, scientists have discovered an exciting and rare phenomenon: an immense chemosynthetic community, likely the largest in the North Atlantic. A chemosynthetic community is one that does not depend on sunlight and photosynthesis. Rather, bacteria create energy by metabolizing gases, such as methane or sulfides, that bubble through the ocean floor. ## 12 major rivers

Major rivers emptying into the Bay include the James, York, Rappahannock, Potomac, Patuxent, Patapsco and Susquehanna from the west and the Pocomoke, Wicomico, Nanticoke, Choptank and Chester from the east.

## 10,000 years old

The Chesapeake Bay was formed about 10,000 years ago when glaciers melted and flooded the Susquehanna River valley.

Bay Geography

## 12 miles wide

The mouth of the Chesapeake Bay is about 12 miles wide between its northern point near Cape Charles, Virginia, and its southern point close to Cape Henry, Virginia.

Bay Geography

## 174 feet deep

The deepest part of the Bay, located southeast of Annapolis near Bloody Point, is called “The Hole” and is 174 feet deep.

Bay Geography

## Remnants of an ancient river

A few deep troughs run along much of the Bay’s length and are believed to be remnants of the ancient Susquehanna River.

## [Largest estuary in the United States]

The Chesapeake Bay is an estuary: a body of water where fresh and salt water mix. It is the largest of more than 100 estuaries in the United States and third largest in the world.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Not to be confused with [Milwaukee].

Deepest part of the Atlantic Ocean; part of the Puerto Rico Trench

![Image 5: Show location on an interactive map]WikiMiniAtlas

[19°35′N 66°30′W / 19.583°N 66.500°W / 19.583; -66.500]

**Milwaukee Deep**, also known as the **Milwaukee Depth**, is the deepest part of the [Puerto Rico Trench], constituting the deepest points in the [Atlantic Ocean].[[1]] Together with the surrounding seabed area, known as **Brownson Deep**, the Milwaukee Deep forms an elongated depression that constitutes the floor of the trench. As there is no geomorphological distinction between the two, it has been proposed that the use of both names to refer to distinct areas should be reviewed.[[2]]

[![Image 6: Milwaukee Deep is located in the Caribbean]]

![Image 7: Milwaukee Deep]

Milwaukee Deep

[]

Location of Milwaukee Deep north of Puerto Rico

During the [Five Deeps Expedition], explorer [Victor Vescovo] achieved the first crewed descent to the location on 21 December 2018.[[3]] Media outlets overwhelmingly referred to the area as the Brownson Deep,[[4]][[5]][[6]] while the name Milwaukee Deep was used by others.[[7]] However, likely due to the factors mentioned above, the expedition has not used any particular name to refer to the site of their Atlantic dive.[[3]] It is named for the USS _[Milwaukee] "USS Milwaukee (CL-5)")_, which recorded the first [echo soundings] of the Puerto Rico Trench in 1939,[[8]] and was itself named for the city of [Milwaukee].

[![Image 8]]

Location of the Puerto Rico Trench, [USGS]

Located roughly 76.0 [miles] (122.3[km]; 66.0[nmi]) north of the coast of the [main island] of [Puerto Rico] at _Punto Palmas Altas_ in [Manatí],[[9]][[10]] the maximum depth of the Milwaukee Deep is 8,376 metres (27,480[ft] "Foot (unit)"); 4,580 [fathoms]), as directly measured by Vescovo during his 2018 descent to the deepest point of the Atlantic Ocean.[[3]] The maximum depth of the Milwaukee Deep has also been reported at 8,750 m (28,710 ft; 4,780 fathoms)[[1]] in 1940 by geologist and oceanographer [Thomas Wayland Vaughan], 8,705 m (28,560 ft; 4,760 fathoms)[[11]] in 1954 by John Lyman, professor of [oceanography] at [University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill], and 8,740 m (28,670 ft; 4,780 fathoms)[[2]] in 2014 by the [General Bathymetric Chart of the Oceans] (GEBCO), and 8,526 m (27,972 ft; 4,662 fathoms)[[2]] in 2018 by marine geologist Heather Stewart and marine biologist [Alan Jamieson]. Stewart and Jamieson also reported a maximum depth of 8,408 m (27,585 ft; 4,598 fathoms)[[12]] in 2019 and 8,378 m (27,487 ft; 4,581 fathoms)[[13]] in 2021.

[![Image 9]]

Perspective view of the sea floor of the [Atlantic Ocean] and the [Caribbean Sea]. The [Lesser Antilles] are on the lower left side of the view and [Florida] is on the upper right. The purple sea floor at the center of the view is the [Puerto Rico Trench], the deepest part of the Atlantic Ocean.

## History

[[edit]]

[![Image 10]]_underway,_circa_the_early_1930s_(NH_97979).jpg)

Discoverer ship [USS _Milwaukee_(CL-5)] "USS Milwaukee (CL-5)")

The ocean floor feature is named for the [USS _Milwaukee_ (CL-5)] "USS Milwaukee (CL-5)"), a [U.S. Navy][Omaha class cruiser], which discovered the Milwaukee Deep on February 14, 1939 with a reading of 28,680 feet (8,740 m; 4,780 fathoms).[[14]][[15]] On August 19, 1952, the [U.S. Fish and Wildlife] vessel _Theodore N. Gill_ obtained a reading of 28,560 feet (8,710 m; 4,760 fathoms) at (

### Crewed descents

[[edit]]

[![Image 13]]

Deep Submersible Support Vessel [DSSV _Pressure Drop_] "USNS Indomitable (T-AGOS-7)") and DSV _Limiting Factor_ at its stern

In 1964, the French submersible _[Archimède]_ explored the Puerto Rico Trench to a depth of approximately 8,300 m (27,200 ft; 4,500 fathoms) but did not reach its deepest point.[[3]]

On 21 December 2018 Victor Vescovo made the first crewed descent to the deepest point of the trench in the Deep-Submergence Vehicle [DSV _Limiting Factor_] (a Triton 36000/2 model submersible) and measured a depth of 8,376 m (27,480 ft; 4,580 fathoms) by direct [CTD] "CTD (instrument)") pressure measurements.[[3]] This made the _Limiting Factor_ the deepest-diving operational submersible at the time.[[3]][[16]]
